role: Prep cook on the chopping board at a five-star hotel's Chinese restaurant
headline: Fresh out of a technical college cooking course and up from Chengcheng county in Weinan, a prep cook starting at the chopping board in the Chinese restaurant kitchen of a five-star hotel in Qujiang, Xi'an, quietly set on one day becoming executive chef
unit: The Chinese restaurant of an international-brand five-star hotel in Qujiang, Xi'an (which also cooks the Chinese dishes for the banquet hall)
level: At school you practiced knife work and tossing the wok, and can cut shreds and slices and score decorative cuts. You can cook a handful of home-style Shaanxi dishes, but you have never worked a hotel banquet line, and you have never filled in a single HACCP record
intro: The summer you finished technical college, you carried a set of knives you had saved up to buy onto a coach from Chengcheng to Xi'an. HR gave you two sets of white chef's whites, a staff card and a locker. The head chef walked you to the board furthest back in the kitchen and said: cut me a crate of potatoes into shreds first, let me see. As of today, in the kitchen of this five-star hotel, there is a chopping board that is yours.
salary_note: Estimate: in a five-star hotel kitchen in Xi'an, a prep cook starts at a little over ¥4,000 take-home, with meals and a dorm bed, and social insurance paid on the base wage, roughly the national figure. Once you are head chef or executive chef, an international-brand hotel pays near the top for Xi'an, though not what the same job pays in Beijing, Shanghai or Guangzhou.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Knife work and prep, high-heat stir-frying, and signing off on banquet dishes

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Working out prep lists and purchase requests from banquet bookings and hotel occupancy

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 1 related job listing nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You swipe in at the staff entrance, change, and stand for the morning health check at the kitchen door: the supervisor looks at your hands for cuts, asks whether you've had an upset stomach these last two days, and ticks a box on the check sheet.

Today you're rostered on the Chinese station at the breakfast buffet: the oil-splashed noodle stand. The noodles were pulled by the pastry kitchen; you blanch the greens, scatter the chili flakes, pour the hot oil. At the hiss, a foreign guest holds up a phone and films it.

Back in the Chinese kitchen for deliveries. You check the mutton's color and press it to see it spring back, weigh the free-range chickens one by one, and beside the supervisor you sign your name on the receiving slip, very small.

Prep at the board. For the warm-tossed kidney shreds you split the pork kidneys, cut out the white core, and score them stroke by stroke; the whole chickens for gourd chicken go off to the steamer first, a dish that is boiled, steamed and fried, three times over.

Lunch service. Two tables of tour groups and three business private rooms order at once, and the ticket printer won't stop. You portion to the tickets, clip the order number to each prep tray and push it to the plater; the second wok is already shouting for the next.

In the staff canteen: saozi noodles and a dish of cold vegetables. In the afternoon break you doze for twenty minutes on the bench in the locker room, and in your dream you are still cutting potato shreds.

There's a twenty-eight-table wedding in the banquet hall tonight. Eight cold dishes, ten hot. You and your senior colleague portion it out table by table, load the trolleys ten tables to a trolley, and wheel them into the banquet kitchen.

Close-down. You scrub and sanitize the board, dry the knives one by one, lock them in the knife cabinet and sign them in; what's left in the cold room gets a date label. When you walk out of the staff entrance, the lights on the city wall are still on.

ladder.title: Chopping-Board Cook
ladder.focus: Check in deliveries, break down meat into cuts, do the knife work and portion to the tickets. You move up to the wok on steady knife work, accurate portions, and knowing the menu and the flow of service by heart.

ladder.title: Wok Cook
ladder.focus: Cook on the second and head wok on your own: stir-fry, flash-fry, braise, simmer and poach, and keep a banquet of dozens of tables coming out without chaos. You move up on consistent dishes, speed, and being able to cover the head wok.

ladder.title: Chinese Kitchen Supervisor
ladder.focus: Run one line and the rota for ten or so cooks, watch banquet dishes, test new ones and place orders. You move up on quality, how you lead people, and how well you work with banquet sales.

ladder.title: Chinese Head Chef
ladder.focus: Own the menus, costs and margins, hiring and food safety for the Chinese restaurant and Chinese banquets. You move up on the reputation of the food, hitting margins and keeping a stable team.

ladder.title: Executive Chef
ladder.focus: Run every kitchen in the hotel: Chinese, Western, banquets, in-room dining and the staff canteen, with the budget, purchasing contracts, group audits and the menu seasons. You hold the job on the hotel's food reputation and its business targets.

ai_tasks.name: Working out prep lists and purchase requests from banquet bookings and hotel occupancy
ai_tasks.how: The system combines banquet bookings, conference meals, occupancy and the same week last year, works out how much mutton and how many chickens tomorrow needs, and drafts the purchase request. A person only glances over it and changes a few lines for the weather and last-minute extra tables.

ai_tasks.name: Cold room temperatures, morning health checks, food samples and food safety records
ai_tasks.how: Sensors log the cold room temperature and alarm when it strays, and the tablet reminds you about the health check and sample sheets and files them. Whether the raw meat smells right, or whether someone with a cut on their hand should stay away from the cold dishes, a cook still has to see and answer for.

ai_tasks.name: Costing banquet menus and working out the margin
ai_tasks.how: AI can cost a table at the day's prices, produce the cost card and margin, and suggest which dish to swap to protect the margin. How the menu runs, and which dish can't be swapped, the head chef settles face to face with the client.

ai_tasks.name: Writing the signature dishes up as standard recipe cards and teaching videos
ai_tasks.how: AI can turn an old master's method into grams and steps with Chinese and English notes and a video, so new cooks learn faster. When that ladle of oil goes in and how high the flame should be, someone still has to stand at the stove and show them.

ai_tasks.name: Knife work and prep, high-heat stir-frying, and signing off on banquet dishes
ai_tasks.how: Breaking down meat, decorative cuts, flash-frying over a roaring flame, sending out dozens of banquet tables at once: it all comes down to skill in the hands and judgment on the spot, and the last taste before a dish leaves the pass has to be a person's.

ai_tasks.name: Deciding the dishes, tasting new ones and training apprentices
ai_tasks.how: Whether a new dish goes on, what it should taste like, what guests say about it: a cook has to taste it and decide. Where an apprentice puts his hand and how the knife moves can only be taught hand on hand.

events.e_potato: You cut a whole crate of potatoes into shreds and left them in ice water. The head chef grabbed a handful, held it up to the light, dropped it back in the bowl and said: uneven, use it for staff meals. About the second crate, he said nothing.
events.e_cut: Rushing the wedding prep, you cut your left index finger. The supervisor sent you to the staff clinic to get it dressed and moved you off anything near the cold kitchen for the day; hotel rules say no one with a cut on their hand touches cold dishes.
events.e_dorm: Four to a room in the staff dorm: the bottom bunk is a lad from housekeeping, the top bunk a security guard. The three of you work staggered shifts, and the light in the room is almost never all the way off.
events.e_new_year: Spring Festival is the hotel's busiest time; forty tables booked for the New Year's Eve dinner. For the first time you didn't go home to Chengcheng. After close-down you called your grandfather, and he asked how many cold dishes were on this year's banquet.
events.e_foreign_guest: A foreign tour group wanted to try tearing their own bread for paomo, the mutton-and-bread soup, and the restaurant sent you to show them. You tore and gestured, saying the pieces should be the size of soybeans. One old woman tore very carefully, and at the end held up her bowl to show you.
events.e_audit: The group's food safety auditors came: through the cold room, into the sample cabinet, spot-checking the health check sheets. One sample box on your line had no time on its label, and it went on the report. At the morning meeting the head chef said nothing, only looked at the lot of you.
events.e_burn: At the peak of service a ladle of hot oil spattered your forearm. You ran it under cold water, smeared on burn cream, pulled your sleeve down and kept cooking. The mark never quite faded.
events.e_love: Every time a woman from the banquet office came to go over a menu, she stood by your board a little longer. Once she asked if you could make Chengcheng-style mutton soup. You said yes, and on your day off you borrowed a stove in the staff canteen.
events.e_contest: You represented the hotel at a citywide Shaanxi cuisine competition and cooked fish in milky broth in a hotpot. A judge tasted the broth and asked what time you had started it. You took gold, and the trophy sits on the cabinet in the head chef's office.
events.e_wedding_self: You got married. The banquet was back home in Chengcheng, and your grandfather, past eighty, insisted on cooking the thirteen-dish village feast himself. You worked as his assistant, and his radish shreds were still finer than yours.
events.e_ai_prep: The kitchen got a prep system that writes purchase orders from bookings and occupancy. For the first two months it kept over-ordering mutton for conference meals and the cold room was crammed. Every morning you corrected its list, until it learned.
events.e_pandemic_slow: One year tourism went strangely quiet, and the banquet hall had no weddings for two months running. The hotel put half the cooks on rotating leave on base pay only, and you spent two months steaming buns in the staff canteen.
events.e_child: The day your child was born, the hotel had a dinner for an international conference. You waited outside the delivery room until the small hours, and at seven in the morning you were back at the stove; your senior colleague cooked your dishes all morning.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in Chang'an district. Every night after close-down you ride your e-bike forty minutes south, and by the time you're home your child is asleep. At weekends you buy vegetables at the market downstairs, and the stallholders have no idea what you do.
events.e_vip: An important official dinner, and the guest asked for authentic Shaanxi food. You watched over a braised pork knuckle with the bone in for a whole day, from choosing the meat to steaming it. After the banquet the food and beverage director messaged you: the guest asked who cooked it.
events.e_apprentice: The new apprentice's potato shreds were uneven. You didn't shout. You handed him a crate of potatoes and said: come back when they'll stand up to the light. He cut for a week, and you watched.
events.e_grandpa: Your grandfather died. For the village gathering, you cooked the thirteen-dish feast on your own for the first time, more than twenty tables, in the big iron wok he left behind.
events.e_robot: The staff canteen and the breakfast stations got automatic stir-fry machines: pour in a sauce pack, press a button, out it comes. You went to have a look. The greens came out a good color, they just had no breath of the wok.
events.e_waist: After more than ten years at the stove, your back has started to disobey. On grey days you steady yourself on the range before bending to pick something up. The doctor told you to lift less, and you handed the frozen deliveries over to the young ones.
events.e_old_guest: A guest who stays at the hotel every year finished his warm-tossed kidney shreds and asked the waiter to bring out the cook. He said he had eaten it here once, ten years ago, and it tasted the same.
events.e_young_few: Fewer and fewer young people apply to the kitchen, and the technical college's cooking classes can't fill their places. You went to the college to recruit; half the students were looking at their phones, and the first question was how many days off a week.
events.e_taste: You notice you need a second taste to judge the salt now. You've started letting your apprentice taste first, then hand you the spoon. You hear him out, then you taste.

c_hotel_or_street.title: A hotel, or a viral restaurant
c_hotel_or_street.situation: A classmate from technical college went to a Shaanxi restaurant that blew up online, right by the old Muslim quarter. Base plus commission comes to ¥1,500 more than you earn, only there's no social insurance. He posts kitchen videos in the group chat and asks how many kilos of potatoes you cut a month.

options.label: Stay at the hotel
options.result: You still prep, check deliveries and fill in health check sheets every day. The hotel has a lot of rules, but banquets, tour group meals, the tastes of foreign guests: you got to see them all, one by one.

options.label: Go to the viral restaurant
options.result: The tables there turn over eight times a day; you cook one dish more than a hundred times a night. Your hands got fast, but the menu never changed. Six months on, you realized you hadn't cooked a banquet dish in a long time.

c_cert.title: Sit the Level 4 Chinese cooking certificate or not
c_cert.situation: Hotel HR says anyone with the Level 4 (intermediate) certificate gets ¥300 a month in skill allowance, and supervisor promotions look at it later on. The exam means memorizing food safety and nutrition, and the practical means cooking a set dish on the spot.

options.label: Sign up and sit it
options.result: You spent a month memorizing questions in the dorm. In the practical you drew sweet and sour pork tenderloin; your senior colleague said your batter was too thick, but you passed.

options.label: Skip it, rely on your hands
options.result: You spent the study time tossing the wok in the staff canteen. No certificate, but the days the second wok cook was off, the supervisor put you on in his place.

c_wok.title: The second wok is open: go for Wok Cook
c_wok.situation: The second wok cook has left for another hotel, and the head chef will pick someone from the boards to move up. Your senior colleague has been here two years longer than you, and everyone assumes it's him; your knife work is better than his, and your wok tossing is no worse.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: Every night after close-down you put in an extra hour on the stove. The head chef tested you on three dishes: warm-tossed kidney shreds, gourd chicken, a plain stir-fry of seasonal greens. You got the second wok, and for months your senior colleague was very polite to you.

options.label: Let your senior have it
options.result: He went up to the wok, took you out for barbecue in Xiaozhai, and said he'd teach you the wok later. You stood at the board for another year or more, until your knife work was good enough that you'd never cut yourself with your eyes shut.

c_rotate.title: A rotation in the Western kitchen
c_rotate.situation: The executive chef says the hotel encourages young cooks to rotate, the Western kitchen is short-handed, and would you go for a year. You'd start again from sauces, sous vide and Western plating, and give up your place at the Chinese stove to someone else.

options.label: Go to the Western kitchen
options.result: You learned to reduce a beef jus and use the vacuum sealer and the sous-vide bath, and you had to call out dish names in English. When you came back to Chinese a year later, a roast rack of lamb of yours went on the new menu.

options.label: Stay at the Chinese stove
options.result: You didn't go. That year you worked through the old Shaanxi dishes again and again, and your milky broth got whiter and whiter.

c_city.title: Shanghai, or back to Chengcheng
c_city.situation: A new hotel in Shanghai is poaching cooks, offering forty percent more than you earn now. Your cousin in Chengcheng wants to go in with you on a restaurant in the county town that caters weddings and funerals. And here at the hotel, you've only just found your footing.

options.label: Go to the new hotel in Shanghai
options.result: The guests there are pickier, and plating a dish takes tweezers. The pay went up; you took the high-speed train back to Xi'an every two months, and on video calls your child called you uncle, then corrected it to dad.

options.label: Go home and open a restaurant
options.result: You went back to the county town. The restaurant mostly caters village gatherings, twenty or thirty tables at a time. Lots of people you know, lots of credit too; you don't make much, but every evening you're home for dinner.
options.end: You went back to Chengcheng and opened a restaurant in the county town that specializes in banquet feasts. When a family has a wedding or a funeral, they book a month ahead, and the thirteen dishes are cooked the way your grandfather's generation did them.

options.label: Stay in Xi'an
options.result: You stayed put. That year the Chinese restaurant got a new menu, and three of the dishes were yours.

c_data.title: Write the old dishes up as standard recipes
c_data.situation: The group is opening new hotels in other cities and wants the Shaanxi dishes here turned into standard recipe cards and teaching videos, with you in charge. A few of the old masters aren't keen; they say once you write down what's in your hands, it isn't that taste anymore.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You broke each dish down into grams, heat and time, and at the bottom of every card you added one line: watch the wok, watch the color, listen. When the new hotel opened, its head chef phoned to say that following the cards got them seventy or eighty percent of the way.

options.label: Turn it down, side with the old masters
options.result: The group got someone else to write them, and the old masters later found several mistakes in the grams on the cards. You said nothing and went on cooking.

c_chef_de.title: Apply for Chinese Head Chef
c_chef_de.situation: The old head chef has been moved to the group's new hotel in Chengdu, and the Chinese head chef's job is open. The other applicant is a Cantonese chef poached from a big restaurant in Guangzhou, whose food looks beautiful, and who talks beautifully too.

options.label: Apply
options.result: On tasting day you cooked a gourd chicken and a gold-rimmed cabbage, nothing fancy, and handed in a seasonal Shaanxi banquet menu with cost cards. The general manager ate, then asked one question: you can really hit this margin? You said yes.

options.label: Don't apply, keep your line
options.result: The Cantonese chef got it, and a few dim sum dishes appeared on the menu. You kept running your line, the banquets went out as usual, and you slept better than you used to.

c_teacher.title: Go back to the technical college to teach cooking
c_teacher.situation: The technical college you went to has asked you back as a practical instructor: winter and summer holidays, no dinner service, a fair bit less pay. The admissions teacher says fewer kids apply for cooking every year, and the college needs someone who has come out of a hotel.

options.label: Go back and teach
options.result: You stand in the training kitchen showing a room of sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds how to cut potato shreds, and, the way your old head chef did, you hand them crate after crate.
options.end: You became a practical cooking instructor at the technical college and send off a class every year; a few of them went into hotels in Xi'an, and at the holidays they send you photos of dishes they've made.

options.label: Stay at the stove
options.result: You said a few more years. The admissions teacher left a stack of leaflets, and you took them back and pinned one on the locker room door.

c_exec.title: Executive Chef at a new hotel
c_exec.situation: The group has opened a new hotel in Lanzhou and asks if you'll go as executive chef. You'd run five kitchens, Chinese, Western, banquets, in-room dining and the staff canteen, and carry the business targets with the general manager. Your family is all in Xi'an.

options.label: Go to Lanzhou
options.result: Every day you read the food and beverage reports first and the kitchens second, haggle with purchasing for half a day over the price of a kilo of beef, and taste the Western head chef's sauces too. You get back to Xi'an twice a month, and your child says you smell of beef noodles.

options.label: Stay in Xi'an
options.result: You recommended another head chef for the job. You still run this Chinese restaurant, and when you have a minute you go and look over an apprentice's potato shreds.

endings.retire: On your last day you still swiped in at the staff entrance at five-forty and stood for the health check, and the supervisor ticked the box, the same as more than thirty years ago. At lunch you didn't work the wok; beside the board you cut a crate of potatoes into shreds and put them in ice water. After close-down you dried the set of knives you'd carried from Chengcheng, and instead of locking them in the cabinet you wrapped them in a cloth and took them home.
endings.burnout: At a wedding banquet one summer, standing at the stove, your vision went black, and your apprentice helped you out to sit by the back door. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You handed in your resignation and went back to Chengcheng. When a family in the village holds a gathering, they still sometimes ask you to come and look over the feast.

stages: Your work starts with deliveries: checking the mutton with the supervisor, weighing the free-range chickens, signing the receiving slip. Then breaking down the meat: from a side of lamb ribs, what roasts and what stews; pork kidneys scored in a wheat-ear pattern; each portion weighed, the prep tray clipped with its order number and pushed to the plater. Board, slicing cleaver, digital scale, cold room labels: that's everything in your hands, and when the woks shout, you have to be ready to pass it up.

You're on the second wok, later the head wok. The ticket printer chatters, the plater pushes the prepped plate across, and you read the ticket, oil the wok, pass the meat through warm oil, flash-fry, thicken. Warm-tossed kidney shreds live or die on those few seconds of blanching; gourd chicken going into the oil, you listen to the sound. With twenty-odd banquet tables firing at once, all that links you to the pass, the board and the plater is shouting, and one call of "service!" decides a dish.

You run the Chinese line, ten or so cooks: the rota, the order sheets, the five-minute briefing before every service. Banquet sales come to you with clients' requests to go over menus; you work out quantities and the order of dishes and write it on the whiteboard at the pass. You cook less now and stand at the pass more, and when a plate's color is wrong, you stop it with a raised hand.

The Chinese restaurant and the Chinese banquets are yours now. Every quarter you sit down with the food and beverage director to revise the menu, and every dish starts with the margin on its cost card; hiring, assigning and appraising cooks is you too. When the group's food safety auditors or the fire inspectors come, you walk them through the kitchen; for an important dinner, you still step up to the head wok and cook that table yourself.

You run five kitchens and more than sixty cooks across the hotel: Chinese, Western, banquets, in-room dining, the staff canteen. Every Monday you meet the general manager and the food and beverage director about cost ratios and guest scores; once a year you negotiate contracts with suppliers, to receiving standards you set. In the tall white hat you walk from kitchen to kitchen, tasting the Western sauces and the staff canteen's saozi noodles alike.
work: Half a lamb came in this morning, and you broke it down to the diagram your senior colleague drew on the whiteboard: ribs, legs, neck, each in its own tub, the scraps kept for the staff meal's minced topping. On the scales, the yield came out a little better than last week.

The wedding's cold dishes need carved roses of red-hearted radish. You carved ten, and your senior colleague picked out three and dropped them back in the basket: petals too thick, the light shows it.

The plater was off in the afternoon, and you covered his station for half a day. When the head wok cook turned round, you already had the prepped bowl of aromatics in his hand. He said nothing, and nudged the wok a little toward you.

A table of foreign guests at lunch ordered kung pao chicken, not spicy. You swapped the dried chilies for a little sweet pepper and served the peanuts on the side, and the waiter said that table wiped their plates clean.

The wedding needs twenty-eight pots of fish in milky broth at once. You start the stock at three in the afternoon, pork bones and chicken frames boiled until it turns white. When the banquet opens, twenty-eight little hotpots are lit together, and the hall fills with white steam.

The head wok cook was off, and you covered the head wok for a night. A braised pork knuckle came out of the steamer and a chopstick slid straight through; you poured the sauce with a steady hand, and not a drop hit the rim of the plate.

For a fifty-table conference banquet, you go over the running order a day ahead with banquet sales, the board and the cold kitchen: when the cold dishes go, when the hot ones fire. You write it on a big sheet of paper and tape it up at the pass.

The broccoli from the new second wok cook came out yellow. You picked up a floret and looked at it: blanched too long, oil too cool. You had him tip it out and do it again, and stood beside him until the second plate was done.

At the month-end stocktake, you find beef wastage is ten percent higher than last month. You pull the receiving slips and the output records and go through them line by line, and in the end trace it to a box of meat left past its date in the cold room.

For the quarterly menu change, you spread twenty dishes' cost cards on the table; three have margins under sixty percent. You tell the food and beverage director: one changes an ingredient, one changes its method, one comes straight off.
Interviewing a wok cook from an ordinary restaurant, you don't ask how many years he's worked. You have him cook a plate of tomato and egg. When he's done, you take one bite and say: start tomorrow.

A guest on a review site said the gourd chicken was dry. You pulled the output record for that day and found the frying oil had been too hot. At the next morning's meeting, you wrote the oil temperature on the whiteboard.

Three people came for the group's annual audit, checking five kitchens' health check sheets, sample cabinets and cold room temperature curves. You walked them round all morning, and in the end they wrote up just one item, in the staff canteen.

Negotiating next year's contract with the meat supplier, who has raised prices ten percent. You print out every batch's receiving record from the past year, point to seven rejected deliveries, and talk the price back down by half.
The Western head chef has made a new lamb main course and asks you to try it. You take a bite and say: good lamb, but Xi'an guests won't take it this pink. Give it another two minutes.
past: You grew up in a village in Chengcheng county, Weinan. Your grandfather was the village cook for gatherings: when someone married or an old person had a birthday, he took his big iron wok and cooked the thirteen-dish feast for dozens of tables, and you crouched by the stove feeding the fire.

Your score in the high school entrance exam fell short of academic high school. Your father said learn a trade; your grandfather said a cook never goes hungry. You applied to a technical college in Xi'an to study Chinese cooking.
First year was knife work. The teacher had you practice push-and-pull cuts on a wet towel, a whole term of it. You were fast, but never even, and the teacher said you were impatient.

In second year you did a placement at a hotel in Xi'an and saw a five-star kitchen for the first time: stainless steel polished so you could see your face, every cook's knives numbered and locked in a cabinet at night.

You passed the Level 5 (entry) Chinese cooking certificate and got your health certificate. In a practical class you made warm-tossed kidney shreds, and the teacher said it was good enough for competition.
Before the placement ended, the hotel's head chef asked if you'd come back after graduating. You turned down the viral restaurant a classmate had found you and waited for his call.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Xi'an's urban employee pension scheme. The hotel paid in on the base wage with few gaps, so in retirement you get a little over 40% of your last monthly salary; rehiring or teaching at a college brings in a separate income.
scenes: Your first week of retirement you still wake a little after five, take a turn round the morning market at the gate of your compound, spend ages with the mutton seller over which lamb is better, and in the end buy only a kilo.
The hotel asks you back twice a month. You don't cook; you stand by the boards watching the young ones prep, and when someone's knife moves too fast, you reach out and tap the back of his hand.

Your grandson has started primary school, and you pick him up after class and buy him a roujiamo on the way home. He says the school canteen food is bad, and you ask whether it's too salty or not salty enough.
For the first few months back in Chengcheng you barely set foot in the kitchen. You eat what the family cooks and say nothing. One day you can't hold back, take the spatula, and cook the dish again.

Someone in the village holds a gathering and asks you to cook. With two young helpers you send out twenty tables of the thirteen-dish feast in a day, and that night your legs are too swollen to climb onto the kang, the heated brick bed, but your heart is light.

An old colleague from the hotel comes to Chengcheng to see you. He says the kitchen got a batch of automatic stir-fry machines, and half the banquet's hot dishes are machine-cooked now. You ask if there's still any breath of the wok. He says a little.
For the first month after leaving the hotel kitchen, you keep waking after ten at night, the ticket printer still chattering in your ears.
An apprentice you trained has become a Chinese kitchen supervisor. He posts a photo of potato shreds he cut, captioned: my teacher taught me. You like it, then zoom in to check how even they are.

The hotel changed brands, and the Chinese restaurant became a viral restaurant. You took the family to eat there once. Warm-tossed kidney shreds are still on the menu; you ate one mouthful and said nothing.

Lots of kitchens use automatic stir-fry machines now, and the systems work out prep and purchasing. The old banquet dishes that depend on the heat, and the thirteen-dish feasts, still need someone at the stove cooking them one wok at a time.

Your wrists and back ache when the weather turns grey. At New Year you still cook a whole table yourself, and the last dish is always eight-treasure sweet rice, turned out onto the plate, the way your grandfather did.

You take your grandson cycling on the city wall. Passing Qujiang, you point at a building and say there used to be a chopping board in there that was yours. Your grandson asks what a chopping board is.

closing.retire: One morning many years later, you sit on the balcony picking over garlic chives, and before you know it you've taken a knife to them, every piece the same length. Your granddaughter asks why you don't use scissors. Scissors leave the cut end flat, you say.
closing.burnout: Many years later, your nephew cooks for the village gatherings now. You sit on a little stool in the yard listening to the wok, and at one sound you know the oil is hot. You call out, and he answers from behind the stove.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the set of knives you carried from Chengcheng to Xi'an, wrapped in a cloth, the longest blade ground a finger's width narrower. You find a whetstone, sit on the balcony, and slowly sharpen them all afternoon.
